source: Gupta and Li (2024) A Training Data Recipe to Accelerate A* Search with Large Language Models
finding: Heuristic errors hurt A* most near the goal, not at the start. An LLM trained as an A* heuristic also generalises best when trained on nodes near the goal.
numbers: Maze and Sokoban. Noise added to an oracle heuristic in two of three path sections (initial, middle, end). Planner-aware sampling gave on average 9.5% fewer A* search steps than uninformed sampling baselines and sometimes beat models trained on double the data.
quote: A* requires more accurate predictions on search nodes near the goal
limits: Small synthetic domains (maze, Sokoban, sliding tile). Fine-tuned CodeT5-type models, not prompting. Gaussian noise is only one error type.
agent_relevance: Rank quality matters most among the few nodes close to a solution. At S6, spend the check budget on candidates that are nearly finished, not on early branches.

source: Gupta and Li (2024) A Training Data Recipe to Accelerate A* Search with Large Language Models: training splits
finding: Models trained only on the End split generalised best among single splits, and training on all nodes was best overall. A heuristic trained on Middle nodes was often inadmissible: it gave long searches avoided but worse plans.
numbers: Sokoban IID optimal %: All 73.94 (ILR 8.38); End only 80.28 (ILR 2.84); Initial only 82.04 (ILR 6.19); Middle only 56.69 (ILR 9.74). Maze All 97.6% optimal. Higher ILR means fewer expansions, so the optimal-percent figures trade against search length.
limits: Reading of which table row belongs to which train split is from PDF text layout and may be shifted by one row. Treat the pattern, not single cells, as the finding.
agent_relevance: An inaccurate ranker saves work and loses optimality: speed gains from a noisy heuristic are not free. Track both cost and quality when ranking.

source: Gupta and Li (2024) A Training Data Recipe to Accelerate A* Search with Large Language Models: wall-clock
finding: A learned LLM heuristic only pays for its inference cost on hard problems. On easy problems it is slower than plain A*.
numbers: Inverse time ratio above 1 means faster than LLM-free A*. Sokoban OOD about 2.4 to 2.7 for the LLM model; Sokoban IID about 0.26; maze about 0.002. Sokoban searches often exceed 10k expanded nodes; maze mostly 2k to 2.5k.
limits: Model labels in the extracted table are mixed. Conclusion is the authors own: benefit only on hard out-of-distribution problems.
agent_relevance: Do not call a model-based ranker on small branching problems; use it when the tree is large.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Breadth-limited search over LLM thoughts, with the LLM scoring each state, lifts Game of 24 from 4% to 74% (GPT-4).
numbers: Game of 24, 100 problems: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%, CoT best of 100 49%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%. About 60% of CoT samples already fail at the first step.
quote: ToT with a breadth of b = 1 already achieves a success rate of 45%, while b = 5 achieves 74%.
limits: Single model (GPT-4), small test subset. Compute is not matched in the headline numbers: ToT uses many more calls. A simple program later solves all 1362 instances (see Katz et al.).
agent_relevance: Strongest direct support for ranking children at S6 and keeping a beam. The beam effect (45% to 74%) is the evidence for keeping several candidates.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: crosswords ablations
finding: On 5x5 mini crosswords, DFS with LLM pruning beats IO/CoT; removing pruning or backtracking hurts. The heuristic is imperfect: an oracle choice of final state helps a lot.
numbers: Word-level success: ToT 60%, solved 4 of 20 games; oracle best state solves 7/20; no-backtrack ablation 20% word level; IO/CoT under 16% word level. Without pruning it found 4/20 correct solutions, 3 of which pruned ToT missed.
limits: 20 games only. The evaluator marked valid rare words as impossible, so the LLM value function loses correct branches.
agent_relevance: A pruning ranker will cut true solutions. Keep pruned branches recoverable, or only prune on code-checked failure.

source: Katz et al. (2024, v3 2026) Thought of Search: Planning with Language Models Through The Lens of Efficiency
finding: Existing LLM tree-search methods (ToT, RAP and others) are neither sound nor complete and use many LLM calls. Having the LLM write the successor and goal-test code, then running plain BFS/DFS, solves whole datasets at 100% with a few calls.
numbers: Game of 24: all 1362 instances solved (1361 solvable, 1 correctly reported unsolvable) by 5 generated successor functions, 1.92 to 6.83 s total on CPU; about 1.2 LLM interactions for the successor function, 1 for goal test. ToT reported 75% on 100 medium problems. Mini crosswords: all 20 solved, 5.5 to 346 s, 2.4 and 1.4 interactions. ToT with 100 expansions needs about 200 LLM calls per game in the worst case.
quote: we can solve the entire datasets with 100% accuracy with only a few calls to the LLM.
limits: The crossword test assumed 10 candidate answers per clue including the correct one. Heuristic function left to future work for 24. Works where an exact successor function can be written; harder for open-ended tasks.
agent_relevance: Where the state space has a checkable successor function, code beats LLM ranking. Fits G5 (code selects). Use LLM heuristics only where no code check exists.

source: Katz et al. (2024) Thought of Search: soundness and admissibility
finding: Soundness and completeness of A*-type search carry over only when the successor function, goal test and heuristic are code. LLM-produced successors can silently lose soundness.
numbers: Analysis of reviewed methods: LLM calls per run grow with expanded nodes; none has a soundness or completeness guarantee. The paper counts calls with admissible but inconsistent heuristics as a separate case.
limits: Position analysis plus four domains; not a head-to-head accuracy study at matched model.
agent_relevance: Treat any LLM score as an inadmissible heuristic and expect over-pruning or over-trusting.

source: Lehnert et al. (2024) Beyond A*: Better Planning with Transformers via Search Dynamics Bootstrapping (Searchformer)
finding: A transformer trained on A* execution traces plans better than one trained on plans alone, and bootstrapping shortens the search it writes out.
numbers: Sokoban: solves 93.7% of test tasks with on average 26.8% fewer search steps than the A* reference implementation. Trace-trained models beat solution-only models most in the low-data regime and on harder tasks. Over 90% of test mazes need traces thousands of tokens long.
limits: Trained from scratch on synthetic maze and Sokoban. Does not show that prompting a general LLM follows A* faithfully. Bootstrapping used 32 samples per puzzle per round.
agent_relevance: Supports writing out the search trace (open and closed lists) for the model, but only for trained models.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Q*: Improving Multi-step Reasoning for LLMs with Deliberative Planning
finding: Treats reasoning as A* with a learned Q-value model as the heuristic. It beats best-of-N with the same value model, without fine-tuning the policy LLM.
numbers: GSM8K: Llama-2-7b with MetaMath 65.2% base; Q* with PRM and QVM reaches 80.8%. MATH: DeepSeek-Math-7b 50.8% base, 55.4% with Q*; Llama-2-7b on synthetic data 41.9% base. MBPP: CodeQwen1.5-7b-Chat reaches 77.0% with Q*.
limits: Q-value model trained by random rollouts of one policy. Learned value is not admissible and no admissibility test is done. 7B models only. Cell-level numbers for the best-of-N rows could not be read from the extracted table.
agent_relevance: A learned scorer with A*-style selection gives a few points over best-of-N, but needs a trained value model.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Q*: guidance versus verification
finding: Using the value model to guide search beats using it only as a final verifier or to train with PPO.
numbers: Text: with the same PRM or QVM, verification beats alignment (PPO); Q* with constant aggregated utility still beats best-of-N.
limits: Per-cell figures not readable from the extracted table.
agent_relevance: Guidance during search beats judging at the end, when the scorer is trained.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS)
finding: MCTS-style search with an LLM value function mixed with a self-consistency score: V(s) = lambda*LM(s) + (1-lambda)*SC(s). Adds reflection after failed trajectories.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 table includes a 92.7 entry (GPT-4, LATS). HotpotQA: n=5 children per expansion, k=50 trajectories, GPT-3.5.
limits: Uses real environment feedback, which is a check the answer was not fitted to. Many more LLM calls than baselines. Table cells garbled in text extraction, so only the 92.7 figure is noted.
agent_relevance: The value mix of LM score and agreement count is a workable ranking rule; real environment feedback does most of the work.

source: Xiao et al. (2023, v3 2025) LLM A*: Human in the Loop LLM Enabled A* Search for Robotics
finding: LLM supplies heuristics to A* in grid path planning. The authors report near-optimal paths with a smaller search space than A*, and better than a PPO baseline. A purely greedy LLM variant gave shorter searches but worse paths.
numbers: Three runs averaged per map; metrics: search complexity (open plus closed set size), path length, maximum deviation times. Paper says LLM Greedy beats LLM A* on search size, but LLM A* gives smoother paths with fewer back-and-forth moves.
limits: Small grid maps, three runs, no admissibility guarantee, human in the loop. Table values not extracted.
agent_relevance: A greedy ranker is fast but gets stuck behind obstacles; adding path cost g(n) fixes back-and-forth moves.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) Planning in Strawberry Fields: Evaluating and Improving the Planning and Scheduling Capabilities of LRM o1
finding: o1-preview solves easy Blocksworld near perfectly but degrades when the problem is obfuscated or longer. It does not search reliably.
numbers: 600 PlanBench Blocksworld: 97.8% correct. Mystery Blocksworld: 52.8%. Randomized Mystery: 37.3%. 110 harder instances needing 20 to 40 steps: 23.63%. Logistics 94% and Randomized Logistics 52% (200 each). Fast Downward 100% on all sets.
limits: Single lab, o1-preview only, private chain of thought, plans parsed with help from GPT-4o-mini.
agent_relevance: Plan accuracy drops with plan length, so rank at shallow depth and verify with code.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) o1: cost and verifier
finding: Reasoning models cost far more time per instance than a classical planner and give no guarantee. Adding an external verifier (LRM-Modulo) guarantees correctness of what is returned.
numbers: Average time per instance about 40 s (Blocksworld) to 167 s (Randomized Mystery Logistics) for o1 versus about 0.12 s for Fast Downward.
limits: Time depends on API load. Verifier-loop numbers not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Proposer plus verifier beats proposer alone; matches G2 and G3.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
finding: In autonomous mode LLMs produce few valid plans. With an external verifier giving back-prompts, success rises a lot.
numbers: About 12% of GPT-4 plans are executable and goal reaching in autonomous mode. Blocks World with VAL back-prompting reaches 82% within 15 rounds; Logistics 70%.
limits: Position paper that reviews the authors earlier results. Benefit is smaller on obfuscated domains.
agent_relevance: LLM as proposer, code as critic: the same split as our schema. The LLM is a heuristic generator, not a sound ranker.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) Chain of Thoughtlessness? An Analysis of CoT in Planning
finding: Step-by-step prompts for planning help only when the examples match the query class very closely, and gains collapse as problem size grows.
numbers: Blocksworld table-to-stack, GPT-4, 261 instances: zero-shot 3.8%; stacking-specific CoT prompt 59.3%. More general prompts give smaller gains (for example 37.1% and 51.3% in the table for the universal-algorithm prompt, per model).
limits: Two models, synthetic domains. The result is about prompt generality, not search itself. Per-size curves are in figures and were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Prompts saying 'do best-first search' are unlikely to carry over to bigger problems; the program must run the search.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) A* search algorithm
finding: A* with an admissible heuristic returns an optimal solution. With a consistent heuristic no node is processed twice and A* is optimally efficient among admissible A*-like algorithms on non-pathological problems.
numbers: Worst case O(b^d), refined O(C*/epsilon). Weighted A* with h_w = epsilon*h, epsilon above 1, gives a path at most epsilon times optimal. The page states no heuristic-error bound.
limits: Encyclopedia source (the V mark in SUBFIELDS.md). Primary theorems (Hart, Nilsson, Raphael 1968; Dechter and Pearl 1985) not opened here.
agent_relevance: The textbook guarantee needs an admissible heuristic; an LLM score gives none. Weighted A* is the nearest analogue to over-trusting a score, with a bounded cost.

source: Bomer et al. (2026) Algorithmic Prompt-Augmentation for Efficient LLM-Based Heuristic Design for A* Search
finding: Putting the A* code into the prompt (A-CEoH) improves LLM-evolved A* heuristics, which can beat expert-designed heuristics on a warehouse problem and on sliding puzzles.
numbers: Evolution of Heuristics framework; 20 generations from the 20 best heuristics; domains: unit-load pre-marshalling and sliding puzzle. Related work cited: EoH needed 2000 LLM queries versus one million for FunSearch on bin packing. Exact gain percentages not extracted.
limits: The LLM writes heuristic code that is scored by running A*; the LLM does not rank at run time. A cited paper (Sim et al.) is titled 'Beyond the hype: benchmarking LLM-evolved heuristics'; not read.
agent_relevance: Heuristics as code scored by execution is the safe way to use an LLM for ranking; suited to an offline step.

source: Zhao et al. (2023) Large Language Models as Commonsense Knowledge for Large-Scale Task Planning (LLM-MCTS)
finding: Abstract only: an LLM world model as prior and an LLM policy as heuristic in MCTS beat MCTS alone and LLM-only policies on novel tasks. A description-length rule says use the LLM as world model when it is much shorter than the policy.
numbers: Abstract gives no numbers. Compared with GPT-2 and GPT-3.5 policies.
limits: Only the abstract page was read this session.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence until the full paper is read.

source: Dechter and Pearl (1985) Generalized best-first search strategies and the optimality of A*
finding: Not opened. From memory: proves A* is optimally efficient among admissible algorithms using the same information, with exceptions for pathological cases.
numbers: none read

finding: Not opened; fetch failed. From memory: weighted A* can do worse than plain A* when the heuristic has local minima.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: Not opened. Described in Gupta and Li and in Katz et al. as an MCTS method with an LLM as world model; Katz et al. say it is not sound or complete and uses many LLM calls.
numbers: none read directly

agent_relevance: Same lesson as Katz et al.: count LLM calls.

source: Gupta and Li (2024): metrics lesson
finding: A shorter search can come from a worse heuristic, because inadmissible heuristics find suboptimal solutions first. The authors added ILR-on-optimal to compare on equal solution quality.
numbers: Metrics: ILR (inverse ratio of search length), SWC (solution length ratio), Optimal %. Sokoban Middle split ILR 9.74 but only 56.69% optimal.
limits: Metric design is the authors own.
agent_relevance: When we test ranking rules at S6, report quality at equal correctness, not just fewer calls.

source: Gupta and Li (2024): related work
finding: Seeding the LPG planner with an LLM plan works better than a random plan (Valmeekam et al. 2023). The paper claims to be the first coreset-selection study for LLM heuristic learning.
numbers: Qualitative.
limits: Second-hand summary of other work.
agent_relevance: An LLM draft plan as seed that a real planner repairs is a cheap, sound pattern.

source: Yao et al. (2023) ToT: compute-matched comparison
finding: With compute matched by nodes visited, ToT still beats best-of-k CoT, but only for b above 1.
numbers: Best-of-100 CoT 49% versus ToT b=5 74%; IO best of 100 33%; IO + refine (k=10) 27%.
limits: Node counts read from a plot. Tokens per node differ, so cost is not equal.
agent_relevance: Branch ranking adds value over plain sampling at equal node count, but the margin is smaller than the headline 74 versus 4.
